title: Starship Flight Tracker
intro: Every SpaceX Starship integrated flight, from Flight 1 in April 2023 to the upcoming Flight 15, with goals, results, causes, lessons and costs. Times are Netherlands time (CET/CEST).
overview: 14 flights flown, the last one the first to reach orbit; the next is planned as the first catch of both stages.
timezoneNote: Times: local Netherlands time (CET = UTC+1 in winter, CEST = UTC+2 in summer). Starbase is on CDT (UTC-5) in summer and CST (UTC-6) in winter: CET = CST + 7 h.

next.timezone: Starbase is on CST (UTC−6); CET = CST + 7 h
next.plan: Orbit, then return both stages to Starbase for the first double tower catch
next.hardware: Both vehicles static-fired late October; ship rehearsed in the chopsticks in September
next.callout: Liftoff time is not announced yet and SpaceX has no Flight 15 mission page up. The time will be added here in CET once it is published.

laterCaption: Dates are no-earlier-than targets and will move.
laterNote: Musk has also said the flight after Flight 15 could refly the caught vehicles; NASASpaceflight expects Flight 16 to use B23 and S43 instead.
costNote: SpaceX has never published a per-flight cost. All figures here are estimates or programme totals, not a price for any single flight.
notes: Success and failure follow Wikipedia's launch-outcome column; SpaceX counts most flights as successful tests.
V1/V2/V3 follow SpaceX's generation names (Block 1/2/3). Flights 7–11 paired a V2 ship with a first-generation booster.
Times are converted from SpaceX's CT times or Wikipedia's UTC times to Europe/Amsterdam.
Flights 12–14 facts that only appear on Wikipedia or secondary sites are flagged inside each flight.

costs.covers: Outside estimate per test flight (2025 era)

flights.summary: First integrated flight. Cleared the pad, but engines failed, the stack tumbled and never separated.
goals: Clear the pad and fly through max-Q
Ship coast on a near-orbital path, reentry and impact north of Hawaii
achieved: Cleared the pad and beach
Reached about 39 km altitude, the highest of any Starship up to then
failed: Several Raptors out before and during ascent
Loss of thrust vector control; vehicle spun and never separated
Flight termination system took about 40 s to destroy the stack
Pad concrete under the launch mount was pulverised, debris thrown widely
lessons: 63 corrective actions accepted by the FAA
Water-cooled steel flame deflector (deluge) installed at OLP-1
Booster aft-end redesign, fire suppression, upgraded flight termination system
Booster switched to electric thrust vector control; hot staging adopted
firsts: First integrated Starship / Super Heavy launch
flights.faa: Mishap investigation; closed 8 Sep 2023 with 63 corrective actions. Root cause per SpaceX: propellant leaks in the booster aft end caused fires that severed the link to the primary flight computer.
flights.cost: No flight-specific public estimate. Context: Musk said SpaceX would spend about $2B on Starship in 2023 (CNBC, 29 Apr 2023).

sources.title: CNBC: Musk says Starship costing about $2B this year

flights.summary: All 33 engines ran full duration and hot staging worked, but both stages were lost.
goals: Ship coast and reentry north of Hawaii
achieved: All 33 booster engines ran to staging
First successful hot staging
New water deluge protected the pad
Ship reached space (about 148 km)
failed: Booster exploded during boostback
Ship lost about 8 min in, just before planned engine cutoff
lessons: 17 corrective actions (10 ship, 7 booster)
Improved LOX filtration on boosters
Ship moved to electric thrust vector control
Ship LOX venting moved to after engine cutoff
firsts: First hot staging
First Starship to reach space
First flight with the pad water deluge
flights.faa: Mishap investigation; closed 26 Feb 2024. Booster: LOX filter blockage starved turbopumps and one engine failed energetically. Ship: LOX vent led to a leak and fires, loss of comms, then automatic termination.
flights.cost: No flight-specific public estimate. Context: Musk said SpaceX would spend about $2B on Starship in 2023 (CNBC, 29 Apr 2023).

flights.summary: Ship completed its full ascent burn and reentered for the first time, but both stages were lost on the way down.
goals: Ship controlled reentry and Indian Ocean splashdown
achieved: Full ascent on a near-orbital trajectory
Payload door test
Propellant transfer demo
First ship reentry data and live Starlink video from reentry
failed: Booster lost about 460 m above the Gulf when only 3 engines lit for landing
In-space relight skipped
Ship lost during reentry after uncontrolled roll
lessons: Added roll-control thrusters on ship
Further LOX filtration upgrades on booster
firsts: First ship to complete its ascent burn
First ship reentry
First in-flight propellant transfer demo
flights.faa: Mishap investigation opened 14 Mar 2024; closed late May 2024 with a no-public-safety-impact finding. Causes: clogged roll-control valves on the ship; LOX filter blockage on the booster.
flights.cost: No public estimate for this flight.
uncertain: Wikipedia counts this flight as a launch success even though both stages were lost; SpaceX treats it as a test that met most goals.

flights.summary: First time both stages came back under control: booster and ship soft splashdowns.
goals: Booster soft splashdown on a virtual tower
Ship survives reentry and splashes down in the Indian Ocean
achieved: Booster controlled splashdown in the Gulf
Ship survived reentry with a badly burned forward flap and splashed down in the target area
failed: One booster engine lost after liftoff (flight continued)
Severe forward flap damage during reentry
lessons: Forward flaps redesigned and moved leeward
Heat-shield tile and backup layer improvements
Cleared the way for a tower catch on Flight 5
firsts: First controlled splashdown of both stages
Booster jettisoned its hot-staging ring
First flight without an FAA mishap investigation
flights.cost: No public estimate for this flight.

flights.summary: The tower's chopsticks caught the booster for the first time; the ship hit its splashdown target.
goals: First booster return and tower catch
Precise ship splashdown in the Indian Ocean
achieved: Booster caught by the tower arms
Ship landing flip and splashdown on target
failed: None of the major goals; booster chine damage and ship flap heating noted
lessons: Catch tower proven; catch became the default plan for later boosters
Ship heat-shield refinements continued
firsts: First booster catch by launch tower arms
flights.faa: No mishap investigation. Licence issued 12 Oct 2024 after a public dispute over timing.
flights.cost: No public estimate for this flight.

flights.summary: Catch called off for safety, but the ship did the first in-space Raptor relight and a daylight splashdown.
goals: Reentry with tiles removed and a steeper profile
achieved: In-space relight
Ship survived the harsher reentry with minimal flap damage
First daylight splashdown
failed: Catch aborted: tower sensors damaged at liftoff, booster diverted to Gulf splashdown
lessons: Hardened tower sensors and catch-abort criteria
Last Block 1 ship; Block 2 ship next
firsts: First in-space Raptor relight
First daylight splashdown
First payload: a plush banana zero-g indicator
flights.cost: No public estimate for this flight.

flights.summary: Booster caught again, but the first Block 2 ship broke up about 8.5 minutes in.
goals: Debut of the upgraded Block 2 ship
achieved: Booster caught (second ever catch)
failed: Ship lost telemetry about 8.5 min in and broke up; no payload deploy
Debris fell around Turks and Caicos; air traffic disrupted
lessons: Fuel feedlines changed, propellant temperatures and thrust target adjusted
Added vents and a nitrogen purge to the ship's aft 'attic'
firsts: First Block 2 ship
First catch of a second booster
flights.faa: Mishap investigation; closed 28 Mar 2025 (announced 31 Mar). Most probable cause: vibrations stronger than expected stressed propulsion hardware, causing leaks and fires in the aft section.
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Outside estimate: about $100M per launch (BBC, Aug 2025, reporting on this era of test flights).

flights.summary: Third booster catch, but the ship lost several engines and control near the end of its ascent.
achieved: Booster caught despite two engines not relighting for boostback
failed: Ship lost several Raptors after an energetic event in the aft section, lost attitude control and was lost
Debris over the Bahamas; Florida air traffic disrupted
lessons: Raptor hardware changes and added preload on joints
New nitrogen purge and improved drainage in the engine bay
firsts: Third booster catch, the last one before Flight 15's planned attempt
flights.faa: Mishap investigation; return-to-flight determination 22 May 2025, closed 12 Jun 2025. Most probable cause: a hardware failure in a single Raptor led to propellant mixing and ignition in the engine bay.
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Outside estimate: about $100M per launch (BBC, Aug 2025, reporting on this era of test flights).

flights.summary: First reflown booster. The ship reached engine cutoff, then leaked, tumbled and reentered uncontrolled.
achieved: First flight of a reused Super Heavy (29 flight-proven engines)
First Block 2 ship to reach engine cutoff
failed: Payload door did not open; no deploy
Relight skipped
Ship leaked, lost attitude control, was passivated and broke up over the Indian Ocean
Booster lost during its landing burn experiment
lessons: Main fuel tank pressurisation diffuser redesigned and requalified
flights.boosterOutcome: Lost (landing burn experiment; within approved test scope)
firsts: First reflown Super Heavy booster
flights.faa: Mishap investigation (ship only); closed 15 Aug 2025. Most probable cause: failure of the main fuel tank pressurisation diffuser, leaking methane into the nosecone.
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Outside estimate: about $100M per launch (BBC, Aug 2025, reporting on this era of test flights).

sources.title: Ars Technica: why the last two Starships failed

flights.summary: Turnaround flight: first payload deployment, an in-space relight and an on-target splashdown.
goals: Booster engine-out landing test with Gulf splashdown
achieved: All 8 simulators deployed
In-space relight
Booster engine-out landing test and splashdown
Ship splashed down on target despite heavy damage
failed: Visible damage and an event in the engine section during reentry; flaps scorched (no mission loss)
lessons: Validated Block 2 fixes after three failures
Ship 36 had exploded on a test stand on 18 Jun 2025 (pressure vessel failure), delaying this flight by about two months
firsts: First Starship payload deployment
First fully successful Block 2 flight
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Outside estimate: about $100M per launch (BBC, Aug 2025, reporting on this era of test flights).

sources.title: BBC: SpaceX pulls off Starship comeback (cost estimate)

flights.summary: Last Block 2 flight and last from the old Pad 1; every major objective met.
goals: Test the V3 booster landing-burn engine sequence
Dynamic banking manoeuvre that mimics a return to Starbase
achieved: Booster hovered and splashed down after the new landing sequence
8 simulators deployed
Third in-space relight
Banking manoeuvre and soft splashdown on target
failed: One booster engine did not relight for boostback (it relit for landing)
lessons: Landing profile carried over to V3 boosters
Pad 1 retired for rebuild; V3 moved to Pad 2
firsts: Last flight of the second-generation ship and first-generation booster
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Outside estimate: about $100M per launch (BBC, Aug 2025, reporting on this era of test flights).

flights.summary: V3 debut from Pad 2. Ship did well despite an engine out; the booster was lost after a failed boostback.
goals: First flight of V3 vehicles and Raptor 3
Deploy 20 simulators plus 2 modified Starlinks that image the ship
Flap stress and banking tests on reentry
achieved: All 22 satellites deployed; heat shield imaged in space
Ship reached its planned trajectory with one engine out
Flap stress test, banking manoeuvre and two-engine landing flip and splashdown
failed: One booster engine out on ascent
Booster flip went off-axis, partial boostback, hard impact in the Gulf
One ship Raptor Vacuum shut down on ascent; in-space relight reportedly cancelled
lessons: Four corrective actions: engine start-up sequence made tolerant of timing variation
Engine alarm and abort thresholds updated
Hardware changes for relight reliability
firsts: First V3 Starship and Super Heavy
First Raptor 3 flight
First launch from Pad 2
First satellites to image Starship in space
flights.faa: Mishap investigation opened 27 May 2026; closed 13 Jul 2026. Causes: heat effects on booster propulsion components during ascent and erroneous engine alarm settings.
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Programme scale: about $3.0B Starship R&D in 2025 per SpaceX's S-1; more than $15B spent in total (Reuters/Bloomberg, May 2026).
uncertain: Engine counts during the booster failure differ between sources (Wikipedia: 20 of 33 relit; Reuters: 5 did not re-ignite).
SpaceX's recap does not mention the relight; Wikipedia says it was cancelled.

flights.summary: First real Starlink V3 satellites deployed; the ship landed and stayed intact, the booster hit the Gulf hard.
goals: Deploy 20 Starlink V3 satellites on a suborbital path
achieved: All 20 Starlink V3s deployed and contacted (then reentered as planned)
In-space relight
First V3 boostback on all 33 engines
Ship soft splashdown and stayed intact after tipping over
failed: Booster landing burn: only a subset of engines relit, hard splashdown
First attempt on 16 Jul aborted at T-0 (Raptor LOX turbopump pressure, attributed to moisture); one weather delay
lessons: Ship 40 was towed and shipped back to Starbase (arrived 7 Oct 2026) for heat-shield inspection
Booster landing-burn relights remained the weak point going into Flight 14
firsts: First operational Starlink satellites deployed from Starship
First ship to survive tipping over after splashdown
First flown ship returned to Starbase
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Programme scale: about $3.0B Starship R&D in 2025 per SpaceX's S-1; more than $15B spent in total (Reuters/Bloomberg, May 2026).
uncertain: Booster landing-burn engine counts differ between sources.
Ship 40 recovery details are from Wikipedia and secondary reports.

flights.summary: First orbital Starship flight: 26 Starlink V3 satellites delivered, then an early deorbit after an engine issue.
goals: About six orbits (nearly 10 h) then deorbit
Booster boostback to propellant depletion and Gulf splashdown
achieved: Orbit at about 275 km after a single-Raptor insertion burn
All 26 satellites deployed and contacted
First deorbit burn and on-target Pacific splashdown
Booster controlled splashdown, then intentional flight termination demo
failed: One booster engine out on ascent; 31 of 33 relit for boostback, 11 of 13 for landing
One ship Raptor Vacuum shut down early on ascent
Mission cut from about 10 h to about 3 h
lessons: Musk (10 Oct) blamed the Raptor Vacuum shutdown on engine-computer software, not hardware
Booster depletion test fed into return-to-launch-site plans for Flight 15
firsts: First Starship in orbit
First operational payload to orbit
First deorbit burn
flights.faa: FAA licence cleared 27 Sep 2026; no mishap investigation announced.
flights.cost: No flight-specific figure. Programme scale: about $3.0B Starship R&D in 2025 per SpaceX's S-1; more than $15B spent in total (Reuters/Bloomberg, May 2026).
uncertain: Software cause is Musk's statement; no formal report published.
SpaceX's timeline lists the original ~10 h plan; actual splashdown was about 3 h after launch.

flights.dateLocal: NET Fri 13 Nov 2026, time not announced
flights.utc: Starbase on CST: CET = CST + 7 h
flights.summary: Planned first attempt to catch both the booster and the ship at the tower.
goals: Orbital flight with payload (reported as Starlink Group 31-2)
Booster return and tower catch: first V3 and first Pad 2 catch
Ship deorbit, return to Starbase and first ever ship catch
lessons: B22 full-duration 33-engine static fire 25 Oct
S42 single-engine deorbit-simulation burn 26 Oct, 60 s six-engine firing 27 Oct
S42 chopstick fit and quick-disconnect tests at Pad 2 on 11–12 Sep
firsts: Would be the first ship catch and first full recovery of both stages of an orbital-class rocket
flights.faa: Licence modification for return to launch site and ship catch not yet issued (FAA Starship page, as of early Nov).
uncertain: Date is from SpaceX VP Kiko Dontchev at UP.Summit (via Eric Berger / Teslarati); FAA planning slides earlier showed 8 and 12 Nov.
Payload name comes from Wikipedia and is not confirmed by SpaceX.
